sections.intro: Monte Carlo sampling beats exhaustive enumeration when variance matters, and a bug bounty researcher explains how they pick features for authorization testing.

stories.title: Monte-Carlo simulations
stories.summary: Monte Carlo uses randomness and the law of large numbers to estimate quantities hard to compute analytically. Examples include estimating pi via dart-throwing, computing that 3.23% of 12-card SET hands have no sets from 10 million samples rather than 70 trillion enumerations, and modeling retirement portfolios under uncertain returns and inflation. Sampling error drops as 1/sqrt(N), favoring Monte Carlo for high-dimensional problems.
stories.why: Shows when sampling beats exhaustive enumeration and why mean assumptions miss variance-driven outcomes in uncertain systems.
stories.takeaway: Sampling-based methods trade precision for tractability, but variance and sequence of inputs matter more than averages alone.

stories.title: How one bug bounty researcher chooses the features they investigate
stories.summary: Researcher @vaib25vicky picks hard-to-understand GitHub features, explores them as a normal user, and watches for misuse paths, specializing in authorization and access control. GitHub restructured its bounty program around quality over quantity, offering VIP payouts up to $30,000 for critical findings. AI tools boost productivity but still require human verification.
stories.why: A bug bounty researcher explains how they pick complex features for authorization testing, useful for engineers building access control.
stories.takeaway: When auditing access control, prioritize complex features and exercise them as users would, watching for misuse paths.

sections.name: papers
sections.label: Papers
sections.intro: RiftANN pipelines ANN search over RDMA-disaggregated memory for billion-scale vectors, and CXDVirt emulates CXL-SSDs inside a kernel module without VM overhead.

stories.title: RiftANN: Efficient Graph Traversal for Vector Search with RDMA-Based Memory Disaggregation
stories.summary: Graph indexes for approximate nearest neighbor search exceed DRAM at billion-scale vectors. RiftANN runs graph traversal across disaggregated memory by navigating with compact vectors locally, batching one-sided remote reads, evaluating returned neighbors in parallel, and using an impact gate to advance traversal when unfinished evaluations are unlikely to matter. On SIFT, SPACEV, and DEEP at 100M vectors plus SIFT1B, it achieves 1.6x-4.3x lower latency and 1.1x-2.2x higher throughput than DistVS at matched recall.
stories.why: Billion-scale vector search breaks single-server RAM; RiftANN makes disaggregated-memory ANN fast via RDMA pipelining and parallel evaluation.
stories.takeaway: For memory-disaggregated search, hide remote latency with batched RDMA pipelines and speculatively advance using thresholded, impact-gated candidate updates.

stories.title: CXDVirt: Low Latency Kernel Module Based CXL-SSD Emulation
stories.summary: CXL-SSDs expose flash with memory-like access and a small DRAM cache, but emulating them in a VM (Cylon) adds over 3 microseconds per cache miss, more than the NAND read itself. CXDVirt runs as a kernel module using devdax and a custom page-fault handler, cutting miss latency 1.4-1.6x (4.1x at P99.9) and scaling better under thread load.
stories.why: Emulating CXL-SSDs in a kernel module avoids VM overhead, useful for anyone building or testing memory-semantic storage systems.
stories.takeaway: Kernel-level page-fault handling can emulate memory-semantic devices without paying VM exit overhead.

sections.name: tools
sections.label: Tools
sections.intro: Ducklake layers time travel and CDC onto plain Parquet, and Rgpu exposes a remote NVIDIA GPU as a PyTorch device.

stories.title: DuckDB Ducklake
stories.summary: DuckLake is a DuckDB extension for an open lakehouse format that stores metadata in a SQL catalog (DuckDB file, PostgreSQL, or SQLite) and data in Parquet files. It supports standard SQL, updates, schema evolution, time travel via snapshot versions, change data feeds, and deletion vectors.
stories.why: Adds database features like time travel, updates, and CDC to Parquet-based lakehouse storage without proprietary formats.
stories.takeaway: Separating metadata into a SQL catalog while keeping data in Parquet enables DBMS-style features on lakehouse data.

stories.title: Show HN: Rgpu – a PyTorch device whose tensors live on a remote GPU
stories.summary: rGPU offers two paths: a PyTorch device running torch ops over TCP against a remote GPU, and a CUDA shim intercepting libcuda, CUDA Runtime, cuBLAS, cuBLASLt, and cuDNN calls. Transport is plain TCP with no authentication or encryption, so users must rely on SSH tunnels and a host firewall on port 9713.
stories.why: Lets you run PyTorch or CUDA workloads against a remote NVIDIA GPU, exposing internals of driver API remoting.
stories.takeaway: Driver-API-level GPU remoting is feasible; the security model here is delegated entirely to SSH and firewall configuration.

sections.name: discussions
sections.label: Discussions
sections.intro: A tiny cross-platform speech-to-text engine shares its C++ inference stack with an LLM, plus a Rust programmer's catalog of C footguns.

stories.title: Whistle: Speech to Text in 16.9 MB
stories.summary: Whistle is a CPU-only speech-to-text model in one 16.9 MB file with no dependencies, running up to 30 s clips across 7 languages. On an M4 Pro it hits 11.1 ms time-to-first-token and 1,319 decode tokens/s, beating Whisper base (145.3 MB) on LibriSpeech, SPGISpeech, Earnings-22 and FLEURS, while sharing its encoder-decoder blocks, quantisation and C++ container with Needle.
stories.why: On-device speech recognition in a single 16.9 MB file, sharing one C++ inference engine with an LLM across 17 platforms.
stories.takeaway: A tiny on-device speech model can share a single quantised runtime with an LLM and still beat a 145 MB baseline on most benchmarks.
stories.debate: Commenters report Whistle getting stuck outputting 'Thank you' as a placeholder and getting only 70/170 right versus qwen-ASR 1.7B's 168/170, while others ask for Parakeet comparisons and live streaming output.

stories.title: C for Rust Programmers
stories.summary: A Rust developer catalogs C's surprising behaviors: booleans only became real primitives in C23, strings end with null bytes unlike Rust's 16-byte length-tagged references, long is 64-bit on Unix but 32-bit on Windows, errors use magic integers plus errno, and arrays silently decay to pointers when passed across functions.
stories.why: A Rust programmer catalogs C footguns like null-terminated strings, platform-dependent integer widths, and array decay to pointers.
stories.takeaway: When reading C code, use fixed-width types from stdint.h for portability and remember arrays become pointers across function boundaries.
stories.debate: Commenters argue these quirks stem from history and compatibility constraints, and that tools like FilC can compile C with safety exceeding Rust's, while garbage collectors often integrate easily.

sections.name: offbeat
sections.label: Off the clock
sections.intro: Archaeologists reconstructed a 35,000-year-old invisible technology from spiral grooves cut into a stone tool, showing how durable artifacts reveal perishable knowledge.

stories.title: Archaeologists Are Reconstructing the 'Invisible' Technologies of the Stone Age
stories.summary: A 35,000-year-old ivory rod with spiral grooves turned out to be a rope-making tool, producing 16 feet of fiber in ten minutes. Stone tool wear marks suggest fiber hafting dates back 250,000 years, but organic materials rarely survive, leaving over 90 percent of daily prehistoric life invisible in the record.
stories.why: A tool's spiral grooves revealed a 35,000-year-old invisible technology, showing how durable artifacts can encode information about perishable systems.
stories.takeaway: Durable artifacts often preserve traces of perishable technologies, so absence of evidence is not evidence of absence.
stories.debate: Commenters speculate about other lost technologies like better fabrics, waterproof clothing, and wooden tools, wondering how much actual sophistication of the Stone Age remains unknown to us.
